Abstract

Geometric spatial reasoning underlies applications from robotics to automated design, yet the ability of large language models (LLMs) to turn a verbal description into a physically connected three-dimensional assembly remains largely underexplored.

Brick assembly is a demanding constructive probe of this ability: a short, underspecified prompt leaves dimensions, proportions, and part layout implicit, and a valid answer must match the semantic intent of the prompt while completing this geometry with discrete pieces that interlock through studs.
We study this setting as the \texttt{Text-to-Brick} task and present BrickForma, a framework that builds training data for a compact model using LLM-assisted parametric programs.

Parametric programs written with large language model assistance generate 80,000 source voxel models across 21 categories on a $48^3$ grid, each described at five levels of detail, yielding approximately 400,000 caption records that tie varying amounts of language to shared geometry.

A voxel-to-brick conversion pipeline with connection analysis and local refinement turns these shapes into geometrically checked brick targets, on which we fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B with low-rank adaptation to predict brick dimensions and positions from text.
A mixed-integer linear programming stage then seeks an exact cover of the voxel target reconstructed from these predictions with a single stud-connected component.
On 525 shared prompts spanning five description levels, BrickForma's raw outputs achieve the highest mean VQAScore, PE, and SigLIP2 at every level among the three systems.
BrickForma has a mean invalid-placement ratio of 0.79\%, compared with 0.00\% for BrickGPT and 18.42\% for BrickNet.
These results support using executable generators and geometric checks to train compact text-to-brick models.
Introduction
Spatial reasoning and geometric understanding are fundamental to human cognition and to artificial intelligence, supporting applications from robotics and navigation to computer-aided design.
As large language models (LLMs) have matured, a growing body of work asks whether they can reason about shape, position, and transformation.
Recent benchmarks probe LLMs' ability through
paper folding and unfolding~\cite{zhou2026paperfoldingpuzzle} and geometry expressed as procedural drawing code~\cite{luo2026geogrambench}.
Each reports pronounced deficiencies in current models.
These studies largely assess spatial reasoning by asking a model to select or compute an answer.

A complementary and less examined question is whether a language model can \emph{construct}: given only words, can it produce a three-dimensional object whose parts are correctly sized, correctly placed, and physically joined?
Lego brick assembly makes this question concrete.
A concise narrative request such as \emph{a simple chair} identifies an object category while leaving its dimensions, proportions, and part layout largely unspecified.
Answering it requires three coupled forms of geometric spatial reasoning.
The model must complete the missing geometry from prior knowledge of what the object looks like.
It must discretize that geometry into pieces of fixed dimensions at integer positions on a grid.
And it must respect the difference between spatial adjacency and stud connectivity, since pieces that touch side by side do not hold together unless they interlock vertically through studs.

We refer to this setting as the \texttt{Text-to-Brick} task: the translation from a natural-language description, at any level of detail, to a set of (Lego) brick placements that reproduces the described shape as a single connected assembly.
Because every output can be checked for coverage, bounds, and connectivity, the task provides a verifiable test of whether linguistic knowledge has become spatial structure.
Prior work has established that language models can be trained for this task.
BrickGPT~\cite{brickgpt} learns autoregressive brick-placement sequences and incorporates validity checks with physics-aware rollback during inference.
BrickNet~\cite{bricknet} adopts a graph-based representation supporting a broader range of parts and connection types.
Two questions remain open alongside these advances.
\textbf{(Q1)} How well do generators translate \emph{limited} linguistic information into object geometry?

In our five-level benchmark (Table~\ref{tab:level-results}), BrickNet obtains lower mean VQAScore, PE, and SigLIP2 than BrickForma at the two shortest description levels, L1 and L2, a gap that only level-wise evaluation makes visible.
\textbf{(Q2)} Can LLM-assisted programs encode the geometric details omitted from concise prompts in a form suitable for training a compact model?
We present BrickForma, which uses executable programs to generate training examples for a compact text-to-brick model.
With GPT-6.1 Sol assistance, we develop parametric programs that vary object proportions, part dimensions, openings, and support arrangements to synthesize voxel shapes in batches.
Each program specifies the structure of an object family and exposes its geometric degrees of freedom as parameters.
The source collection contains 80,000 models across 21 categories on a $48^3$ grid.
Each model is paired with five levels of description that progressively introduce structural, geometric, proportional, and appearance information.
The resulting approximately 400,000 caption records link concise requests and detailed specifications to shared geometry, providing supervision for prompts with different amounts of geometric detail.
Turning voxel shapes into brick targets is where spatial adjacency and stud connectivity must be separated.
Pieces can cover a connected voxel volume and touch side by side without forming stud connections.

Our conversion pipeline combines same-color brick placement, connection analysis, and local refinement to construct geometrically checked target layouts, with changes to source voxels recorded in derived models.
The integrated dataset release includes 79,301 models passing its dataset-level geometric checks.
We fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B~\cite{qwen3} with low-rank adaptation~\cite{lora} on caption--placement pairs to predict brick dimensions and spatial positions.
Geometric refinement complements the small model's predictions with explicit structural enforcement.

From the supported, in-bounds portions of predicted placements, the pipeline forms a voxel union and uses mixed-integer linear programming to seek an exact-cover layout forming a single stud-connected component.
Independent coverage and connectivity checks verify the refined layout.
This design assigns the two halves of the task to the components suited to them: the language model decides what shape a description denotes, and the solver decides how that shape holds together.
We evaluate BrickForma against BrickGPT and BrickNet on 525 shared prompts spanning five description levels.
BrickForma's raw outputs achieve the highest mean VQAScore, PE, and SigLIP2 at every level, including the shortest descriptions.
BrickGPT has the lowest mean invalid-placement ratio (0.00\%), followed by BrickForma (0.79\%) and BrickNet (18.42\%).
Reporting all five levels connects the multilevel data design to an explicit assessment of how generation changes with the amount of descriptive detail.
In summary, the main contributions of this work are as follows:
LLM-assisted construction of training data for a compact model.

On the 525 shared prompts, BrickForma attains a 30.0\% higher mean VQAScore than BrickGPT.
A multi-level dataset that enables experimental validation of small language model alignment across various levels of descriptive detail.
With our LLM-assisted parametric data construction pipeline, we generated 80,000 source voxel models with five description levels each.
In the integrated release, 79,301 of the 80,000 source models yielded brick layouts that passed the geometric checks.

We fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B on caption--placement pairs and carried out level-wise evaluation against BrickGPT and BrickNet to assess text--image alignment and invalid placements across descriptions ranging from concise prompts to detailed specifications.

Related Work
Brick assembly and generation.
Prior work formulates brick assembly as graph generation, sequential construction, or structural understanding~\cite{thompson2020lego,brickbybrick,breakandmake}.

BrickGPT~\cite{brickgpt} predicts autoregressive placement sequences and validates candidate bricks during decoding, while BrickNet~\cite{bricknet} adopts an assembly-graph representation over a broader catalog of parts and connectors.

Rather than relying solely on autoregressive decoding or graph prediction to maintain structural validity, BrickForma predicts absolute grid placements for rectangular footprints and delegates global stud connectivity to exact-cover voxel reconstruction.
Stability analysis.
StableLego introduces a force-balance model to evaluate block-stacking assemblies~\cite{stablelego}.

In BrickForma, inference-time refinement enforces stud connectivity and exact voxel coverage, while our dataset-level contact screening applies complementary force and ground-contact assumptions to flag physically plausible structures (Appendix~\ref{app:dataset}).
Procedural data and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
Procedural generation enables systematic control over shape diversity and dataset scale~\cite{infinigen}.

BrickForma leverages an LLM to author executable parametric generators, verifies their geometric outputs algorithmically, and fine-tunes a compact text-only model on the resulting caption--placement pairs via LoRA~\cite{lora}, adopting BrickGPT's serialized placement representation~\cite{brickgpt}.
Dataset Construction
Parametric Voxel Generation

To crystallize broad geometric priors into explicit supervision, GPT-6.1 Sol assists in authoring analytic parametric generator programs across 21 object categories, each partitioned into 40 structural families (47--48 instances per family in each 40,000-model shard).

For every instance, a planning module samples independent design parameters---governing category-specific components, proportions, openings, and support structures---and deterministically rasterizes the geometry onto a $48^3$ grid ($Y{=}0$ ground contact) while deriving L1--L5 captions from the same underlying plan.

Rather than applying random cell deletion, cavity filling, or post-hoc bridges, density adjustments regenerate the entire shape from its continuous parameters until automated checks confirm 750--1,250 occupied voxels and a single six-neighbor connected component.

Exact and canonical occupancy hashes across 48 axis and sign transforms verify zero cross-shard duplicates, with geometry plans and version identifiers preserved alongside each record (Figure~\ref{fig:data-workflow}, where \texttt{shape(params)} denotes the analytic shape and \texttt{emit(x,y,z)} records occupied voxel coordinates).
BrickForma-48 (archived under \texttt{BrickMore-48} in the accompanying dataset and checkpoint releases) pairs each shape with five bilingual descriptions.

L1 names the object and its primary parts, whereas L2--L5 progressively layer structural, proportional, appearance, and viewpoint details onto the exact same source geometry (see Appendix~\ref{app:dataset} for a birdhouse example).
Voxel-to-Brick Conversion and Checks
Converting a connected voxel volume into a buildable brick target requires separating mere spatial adjacency from vertical stud connectivity.
Our pipeline tiles each layer with same-color rectangular bricks and analyzes the resulting stud-connected components.

When ungrounded fragments arise, local refinement modifies the layout while logging all voxel edits against the source shape, raising the geometry-pass count from 65,503 to 79,298 (recovering 13,795 failures).
Across the corpus, refinement adds 228,582 voxels and removes 125, while 31,532 passing models require no edits at all.
For challenging layouts, conversion falls back to layer-wise exact-cover search or a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) that explicitly enforces a stud path to the ground.

A minimum-remaining-values (MRV) heuristic branches on the uncovered voxel with the fewest valid candidate bricks; the initial release also employed bounded beam search when greedy placement failed the geometric audit, ranking partial layouts by uncovered voxels and remaining stud components.
Release-level verification confirms that target voxels form a single six-neighbor component, every brick component is grounded, and the brick assembly exactly covers the derived target.
While multiple independently grounded components may pass release-level checks, inference-time refinement enforces a stricter single-component constraint.

Separately, a self-weight screen evaluates the final assembly and, if feasible, each bottom-up completed-layer prefix, recording the tipping margin and estimating per-stud tensile demand when compression alone cannot balance gravity (Appendix~\ref{app:dataset}).

BrickForma Text-to-Brick Model
Fine-Tuning

We fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA on English L1--L5 captions paired with their checked brick layouts, using a model-level 9:1 split so all five descriptions of a given shape remain in the same partition.
The $48^3$ workspace uses 20 oriented footprints (11 brick sizes up to planar rotation).

Each instruction specifies the allowed brick dimensions, and the target lists one placement per line---such as $2{\times}4\ (x,y,z)$---serialized Y-first and then X, capturing pure geometry without color tokens.
Training follows the BrickGPT Qwen3 recipe~\cite{brickgpt} (Table~\ref{tab:finetune-config}) with unpacked sequences to preserve caption boundaries.
The run completed 133,860 steps in 25.3 hours across eight GPUs.
Validation loss reached its minimum of 0.0308 at step 79,000---which we retain as the released checkpoint---before rising slightly to 0.0339 at the end of epoch 3 (Appendix~\ref{app:training}).
Fine-tuning configuration (details in Appendix~\ref{app:training}).
Inference and Refinement
As outlined in Algorithm~\ref{alg:inference-refinement}, decoding runs with thinking disabled, temperature $0.7$, top-$p$ $0.9$, and a 8,192-token budget across seeds 42, 104, and 2026.

A draft is considered complete upon emitting an end-of-sequence token; the pipeline selects the first completed draft that passes the geometry validator, or otherwise the completed draft with the fewest reported errors.
Any valid raw draft already forming a single stud-connected component is returned directly.

For disconnected or overlapping drafts, we isolate the semantic shape proposal by forming the in-bounds voxel union $C$ of all supported placements (counting overlaps once) and delegate structural assembly to an MILP solver.

The solver seeks an exact cover of $C$ forming a single stud-connected component under time tiers of 12, 60, and 180 seconds, followed by an independent audit of placement validity, coverage, and connectivity.
If the budget is exhausted, the pipeline retains the raw draft and queues a reseed, with optional recovery runs extending the budget to 600 seconds or sampling additional seeds.
Throughout our evaluation, we refer to pre-solver model outputs as \emph{raw} and solver-reconstructed outputs as \emph{refined} (see Appendix~\ref{app:eval} for the exact-cover constraints).
BrickForma inference and refinement
Comparative Evaluation
Setup and Metrics
We evaluate BrickForma against BrickGPT and BrickNet on 525 shared prompts spanning 21 categories and five description levels (105 prompts per level).
Scoring one delivered output per system and prompt yields 1,575 LDraw exports.

To isolate the learned model's geometric quality prior to solver intervention, the main benchmark evaluates all delivered raw BrickForma exports---including incomplete drafts---while Appendix~\ref{app:eval} separately details the refinement diagnostic.
Text--image alignment.
Each export is rendered with uniform yellow material across eight $512{\times}512$ orthographic views spaced $45^\circ$ apart in azimuth at $25^\circ$ elevation.
Alignment scores take the maximum over views and average across prompts.

VQAScore~\cite{vqascore} computes the first-token probability of \textquotedblleft Yes\textquotedblright\ from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct~\cite{qwen25vl}, PE~\cite{pe} measures cosine similarity between normalized image and text embeddings, and SigLIP2~\cite{siglip2} evaluates the sigmoid of the image--text logit.
Invalid placements.
For an export containing $n$ placements in file order, let $I_i$ indicate whether placement $i$ violates BrickNet's inset collision kernel~\cite{bricknet} given preceding placements.
We report the mean per-export invalid-placement ratio $P_{\mathrm{inv}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}I_i$.

Geometric Refinement Audit

Defining stud contacts by footprint overlap across adjacent layers, we map the same 110 pairs onto a grid with 20 LDU horizontal pitch and 24 LDU layer height and align each export to a common occupied-cell origin.

All 110 pairs preserve identical occupied voxel unions after translation, while single-component assemblies rise from 18 to 110 and overlap-free layouts rise from 100 to 110 (Table~\ref{tab:export-audit}).

In the separate 525-prompt diagnostic run, only 46 raw drafts form a single stud component, whereas all 525 final layouts achieve single-component connectivity while preserving their target voxel unions after the recovery procedure (Appendix~\ref{app:eval}).
Evaluation Boundaries

Our benchmark compares delivered exports from systems that differ in inference settings and part libraries, while description levels vary in both semantic detail and token length---truncating 121 prompts in PE and 209 in SigLIP2 (Appendix~\ref{app:eval}).

Uniform yellow rendering isolates geometric form and layout without assessing color fidelity, and the paired refinement audit covers delivered pairs, excluding unsuccessful solver attempts from its denominator.
Limitations and Discussion

Our experiments evaluate the combined data-construction and fine-tuning pipeline; isolating the specific contribution of LLM-authored generators relative to hand-crafted procedural baselines under a matched training budget remains future work.

Moreover, while dataset release checks verify grounding and coverage and inference refinement enforces a single stud-connected component, physical stability and feasible assembly ordering require dedicated structural measurements.
Finally, the integrated dataset release and the fine-tuning run record their sample counts separately (Table~\ref{tab:training-data}).
Conclusion
BrickForma crystallizes LLM-authored parametric programs into checked voxel-to-brick targets to fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B for \texttt{Text-to-Brick} assembly.
On 525 matched prompts spanning five description levels, its raw outputs lead all three text--image alignment metrics while keeping mean invalid placements at 0.79\%.

Paired with exact-cover MILP refinement that enforces stud connectivity while preserving the voxel union, this division of labor offers a practical path toward constructive 3D spatial reasoning in compact models.

They use release-specific versions and criteria and are not substitutes for the integrated statistics or the current main comparison.
Contact-based gravity screening.
We model 8\,mm stud spacing, 9.6\,mm brick height, and 1\,g per occupied stud-brick cell.
Each overlapping stud contributes four vertical contact points at the corners of a square with half-width 0.25 stud.
The horizontal ground can only provide compression at the corners of ground-level brick footprints inset by 0.05 stud.
A linear program (LP) seeks vertical force balance and balance of the two gravity-induced moments for every brick.
We verify the resulting contact forces against these equations.
After the final assembly passes, the same check is applied to the bricks through each completed layer, bottom to top.
Each stud-connected component of a prefix is checked independently on the unanchored ground.
Tipping margin and clutch demand.
The tipping margin is the minimum signed inward distance from the horizontal center-of-mass projection to the edges of the convex hull of the ground contacts.
We convert the margin from studs to meters and reject zero or negative margins within numerical tolerance.
If the compression-only LP is infeasible after this check, a second LP permits tension at internal stud contacts.
It minimizes the largest total tensile force across the four contact points of any single stud.
We report this minimum required clutch force in newtons per stud.
Actual clutch capacity is uncalibrated.
A verified compression-only solution qualifies for a gravity-screening pass, while solutions requiring tensile support are recorded separately.

Inference refinement.
For the clipped voxel union $C$, let $\mathcal{B}(v)$ index candidate placements from the oriented footprint library that cover $v$ and stay entirely within $C$.
With binary placement variables $x_b$, exact coverage requires $\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}(v)}x_b=1$ for each $v\in C$.
This preserves the union and excludes overlaps.

To enforce a single stud-connected component, a standard single-commodity flow formulation routes flow from a virtual root $r$ through directed stud-contact edges $(b,b')\in\mathcal{E}$ across adjacent layers: grounded candidate placements $b\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{gnd}}$ receive root inflow $f_{r,b}\ge 0$, internal edge flows satisfy $0\le f_{b,b'}\le M x_b$ and $0\le f_{b,b'}\le M x_{b'}$ (for capacity bound $M=|C|$), and flow conservation $\sum_{(u,b)\in\mathcal{E}\cup\{(r,b)\}} f_{u,b} - \sum_{(b,v)\in\mathcal{E}} f_{b,v} = x_b$ ensures every selected placement is connected to the root.
SciPy's HiGHS MILP interface uses the time tiers in Algorithm~\ref{alg:inference-refinement}.
A feasible cover must also pass the independent placement, coverage, and connectivity audit.

Diagnostic cohort.
To probe what the fine-tuned model learns, we inspected 525 BrickForma generations from a diagnostic set (21 categories $\times$ five levels $\times$ five phrasings).

The 525-prompt diagnostic batch, together with 105 first-batch prompts, formed the six-phrasing candidate pool from which 45 of the 114 comparison outputs were selected (35 of them from the 525), as described above.
Algorithm~\ref{alg:inference-refinement} describes the default candidate-selection and refinement rules.
The diagnostic manifests record either a refinement tier or a raw layout kept unchanged.
For 28 prompts a recovery path sampled seeds outside $S$; for two further prompts the solver budget was extended to 600\,s.

Only 46 raw layouts (8.8\%) form a single stud-connected component without refinement; this rate shows no clear trend across levels (13, 9, 9, 7, and 8 for L1--L5) but varies strongly by category (e.g., 8/25 for sofa, 0/25 for basket and camera).
All 479 failing raw layouts split into at least two stud components (median 5, maximum 33).
Overlaps are a minor cause: 50 failing layouts contain duplicated voxels, 41 of them with at most five (median 2), and 429 contain none.
The 2,240 detached fragments are mostly not grounded (1,320 airborne versus 920 grounded).

The learned representation thus places bricks whose in-bounds voxel union is retained by refinement but that often fail to interlock across layers; all 525 final assemblies form a single stud-connected component with that union unchanged (Table~\ref{tab:diag} in Appendix~\ref{app:eval}).
These checks evaluate stud connectivity and in-bounds voxel-union consistency, not prompt-level shape fidelity or spatial reasoning.
